title: Lending Solutions Redesign
subtitle: Turning a loan workflow no single team owned into one everyone could see, own and fix
summary: Making an unowned loan workflow visible enough to fix

meta.label: Team

value: ==The Global Private Bank spans USPB (55 U.S. markets) and IPB across APAC, EMEA and LatAm: 1,000+ advisors, clients in 140+ countries, nine languages, 30+ regulators.== Lending is one product line inside that footprint.
I own two of its surfaces: where a loan begins, and where it's managed every day.

blocks.value: Between them sits every role that touches a loan (Bankers, SC Advisors, Lender Specialists, Credit Risk and Middle Office) and every handoff where it can go wrong.

indexedSections.title: The brief, and why it was wrong

value: The brief arrived narrow: the intake form is bad, so clean it up and cut the rework.

blocks.value: The business heard a UI problem. Before redesigning anything, I wanted to know whether it was one.

blocks.label: The reframe
blocks.value: The form wasn't the problem. It collected what the Banker knew, but was judged against what Credit needed. It was a handoff mismatch, not a UI one.

indexedSections.title: Mapping a workflow nobody owned end to end

value: Proving that meant seeing the whole chain, and no one could show it to me. Each role knew its own segment and assumed the next worked. With no documented IA or personas, everyone designed against their own mental model.
Before fixing the workflow, I had to build the foundation it was missing.

blocks.value: I interviewed lenders and domain owners in every role, joining their check-ins and morning meetings to reach the client-facing ones. Then I turned what I heard into two artefacts: an information architecture of the Lending Workspace, from L1 products down to page controls, and personas capturing each role's goals, jobs and pain points.

blocks.label: Impact beyond my project
blocks.value: Both became the team's source of truth. Designers and POs now cite them in their own reviews and roadmaps.

The map showed where the work happened, not where it broke. So instead of more interviews, I put one person from each role in a room with a single anonymised deal printed as a timeline on the wall: a real-estate investor borrowing against existing assets to buy a property. Nobody described their job. We walked that one deal end to end, and each person marked where their own work stalled.

blocks.label: One deal on the wall, with every stall marked by the person who hit it

blocks.value: The same stalls kept recurring, and the most consistent was this: requests reached Credit without the collateral and entity details the Banker was never asked for, the asset basis and ownership structure needed to size the facility.

items.title: NIGO
items.desc: Requests came back not-in-good-order, for the Advisor to fix and resubmit

items.title: Restart
items.desc: An error partway through meant starting the request over from the top

items.title: Handoffs
items.desc: Credit Middle Office chased the missing pieces by email, one at a time

blocks.value: The system rewarded institutional knowledge. Advisors had to already know what Credit would ask, and anyone who didn't paid for it in rework.

blocks.label: The baseline
blocks.value: I audited 40 recent loan requests with Middle Office: ~60% bounced at least once, and missing collateral and entity detail was the reason more often than anything else.

indexedSections.title: Manufacturing an owner for an unowned problem

value: The evidence was clear; the owner wasn't. The workflow crossed four teams in USPB and IPB, each with its own regulators and roadmap. POs owned their slices deeply, but ==nobody owned the seams==, so "fix the intake" bounced between the Loan Request App and Credit.

blocks.title: ==Make alignment a habit, not a meeting==

blocks.value: With a pilot already live in USPB, EMEA and APAC, one workshop wouldn't keep specialised, distributed teams aligned. So I set up three recurring rituals.

items.title: Design office hours
items.desc: Any PO's question, before it became a conflict.

items.title: Socialised decisions
items.desc: The why behind each decision, not just the screens.

items.title: Refinement calls
items.desc: Feasibility issues caught before anything got built wrong.

blocks.label: Why it worked
blocks.value: Alignment isn't a document; it's presence. Being in the rooms where work was scoped made me the link between siloed owners.

value: The rituals kept teams in sync, but not in sequence: every owner could defend their slice, and no one could order the work across all of them.

When leadership called a three-day portfolio workshop at the Ohio HQ, I joined as the only designer among POs, journey owners, data, architecture and risk, walking each initiative through to owner, dependency and sequence.

blocks.label: Three days at the Ohio HQ

blocks.value: I brought prototypes, and they became the room's reference points. The agenda named them. Framing every feature by persona and journey, rather than by system boundary, shaped the Workspace model we left with: persona views and work queues, one experience instead of ten apps.
The three futures I put in front of them:

items.title: One Request, Any Deal
items.desc: no SBL-vs-Custom fork, the split behind mis-routed intake.

items.title: AI Application Agent
items.desc: chat, and the system drafts the ticket.

items.title: Collateral-First Builder
items.desc: start from assets; size, rate and headroom update live.

blocks.title: The three future-vision proposals, side by side
blocks.intro: Switch variants to compare today's Loan Request workflow with the three futures I put in front of the room. These are the prototypes I used to help leadership decide where the product goes next.

blocks.label: Why it mattered
blocks.value: As the only designer at the portfolio table, I helped leadership choose a direction instead of handing design a backlog to decorate.
A direction isn't a release. No PO ran cover: I drove the build across four teams without authority over any of them. What carried it was artefacts, not opinions.

items.title: Prototypes, not specs
items.desc: Clickable flows exposed what specs hid, like an unreadable collateral field. v1 shipped fixes for the costliest stalls and parked the rest.

items.title: Anchored to the baseline
items.desc: “Six in ten get redone” settled every argument.

blocks.value: Regional variants shipped on one skeleton: conditional logic adds what each market requires instead of forking the product. Try both products below.

blocks.title: Loan Request App
blocks.intro: Where a request begins: the banker adds the parties, acts on an existing facility or builds a new deal, and gets an indicative offer, with Credit's rules checked at entry instead of after submission.

blocks.title: Lending Workspace
blocks.intro: The single pane of glass that replaced ten separate apps: the book, the deal pipeline, portfolio health, insights and QC in one shell, organised by who's working and what they're doing rather than by which system holds the data.

items.label: Faster loan request submission
items.desc: New Loan Request App vs. the old one

value: The new Loan Request App is live and in use globally. Clients usually finish the new e-CQ credit questionnaire in about 5 minutes, and sometimes in as little as 3.

Validate-at-source intake brought new-ticket NIGO ==down to ~22% from ~60%==. NIGO (not in good order) is the firm's own term for the bounce-back rework I set out to reduce. It's a programme-level result: the redesign contributed alongside process and training changes.

blocks.label: In their words
blocks.value: Pilot users called the new Loan Request App “much smoother,” “super easy to use” and “a big improvement” on the old one.

The Workspace gained coherence too: the Deal Journey Tracker now integrates the eCQ credit questionnaire and covers IPB SBL and Custom deals, giving end-to-end visibility across the seams I mapped. And the IA and personas remain the team's source of truth.

indexedSections.title: Ownership problems in a design costume

blocks.label: The takeaway
blocks.value: The hardest problems here weren't design problems. They were ownership problems in a design costume. My job was to make the invisible visible until the right call became obvious.
Three moves proved repeatable beyond this project:

items.label: Move 1
items.title: Build the source of truth
items.desc: My IA and personas still anchor how the team works.

items.label: Move 2
items.title: Make the problem undeniable
items.desc: Six in ten requests bounced; after that, nobody argued.

items.label: Move 3
items.title: Design upstream
items.desc: Prototypes gave leadership something to decide against.

blocks.value: What I'd do differently: wire telemetry into the stalls we targeted from day one, so the NIGO improvement attributes cleanly to the design change, and the parked work has evidence ready when it's next up for prioritisation.
